recipes.name: St. Patrick's Day Deviled Eggs
ingredients_raw: 2 small stalks celery from the heart, minced
2 drops green food coloring, or as desired

steps.text: Place eggs in a large saucepan and cover with water. Bring to a boil, remove from heat, and let eggs stand in hot water for 15 minutes. Remove hard-cooked eggs to a large bowl of cold water or the refrigerator and let sit until eggs are cold, at least 30 minutes
Prepare egg dye according to package directions in a large metal or glass bowl.
Gently crack eggs but do not remove shells so egg dye can reach egg whites.
Working in batches, place cracked eggs into dye until it seeps through the cracks and colors eggs slightly, about 5 minutes per batch.
Rinse eggs and peel to expose the green marbled color; slice eggs in half lengthwise.
Scoop egg yolks into a medium bowl and mash with a fork. Mix in celery and mayonnaise until well combined; stir in green food coloring.
Spoon yolk mixture into egg halves; top each egg half with a parsley leaf.

raw_recipe.headline: St. Patrick's Day Deviled Eggs
raw_recipe.description: These green deviled eggs are perfect for St. Patrick's Day. Each marbled egg half is filled with light green yolk filling and topped with a parsley leaf.

review.reviewBody: No offense to the author of this recipe, but after reading the difficulty some had getting the dye to penetrate the membrane for green marbelizing, I'd like to offer another option instead that I use successfully. I get that it alters the recipe as shown, which is why I offered a middle of the road rating. After peeling the eggs and removing the yokes, I use a spoon to carefully place 3-4 of the whites at a time into cups of the green dye/warm water/vinegar mixture and let them sit anywhere from 5 minutes to the point where they've reached the shade of color you want. I gently move them around a couple times to make sure they color evenly, then remove them to dry completely upside down on paper towels before filling them. They won't be marbleized, but they'll be green! Then you can decide if you want to also dye the yokes green or leave them their natural yellow. I've done this for years on St. Paddy's Day and I do the same with pastels for my Easter presentation. (To get the deepest colors, be generous with the amount of dye you add.) May the luck of the Irish be with you!

This is a fun idea! Everyone at our gathering loved it. I plan to repeat it for Easter with pastels. Easy to do if you plan ahead for the dye to adequately color the egg whites. I let them sit overnight. But next time I'll make the yolk filling more interesting this time with some of the traditional ideas for deviled eggs.

Not as easy as stated! Getting the marbled effect for the whites was far from easy & required far more effort than these directions noted. I had to take cuticle scissors & cut through the membrane - following some of the broken shell marks - before soaking to get anything like what was pictured. Way way too much work.

I made my egg dye using 1 cup warm water & 1/4 cup white vinegar + green food color. My eggs must have had really thick membranes because even though I thoroughly cracked the shells the dye didn't soak through to the egg white except for in a couple of places. WARNING - if you want to pipe the filling into the eggs do not use a star tip - the celery plugged the tip - I pushed a little too hard to try and clear it and ended up with a green egg yolk explosion. As for the filling it needs to be kicked up a notch. Thanks for a fun idea - it just didn't work out too well for me.
